grades.quote: The basic plan is for the parent and child to initially share all physical pages, but for each to map them read-only (with the PTE_W flag clear). Parent and child can then read from the shared physical memory. If either writes a shared page, the RISCV CPU raises a page-fault exception.
grades.reason: Directly explains COW fork. Parent and child share physical pages mapped read-only. A write causes a page fault. The kernel then copies the page and gives the faulting process a private writable copy, so neither can overwrite the other.

grades.quote: Neither process has permission to write into the shared area. If either violates this restriction, the operating system copies the affected page, gives each process write permission for its own copy, and allows the write operation to proceed (Step 3).
grades.reason: Describes the general COW mechanism: shared pages are read-only, and a write triggers a page copy with private write permission. It is framed around message passing, not fork, but the isolation principle is the same.

grades.quote: The operating system maps the text into each process’s virtual memory address space, with the protection bits in the MMU set to enforce read-only access.
grades.reason: Covers sharing memory between processes with read-only MMU protection, which is background for COW. The visible text does not reach copy-on-write or fork, so it answers little of the question.
Covers fork/exec usage and POSIX API. It says nothing about copy-on-write, page sharing, or protecting parent and child memory.
